title: ISO/IEC 42001 and ETSI EN 304 223
body:
ISO/IEC 42001 addresses an organisation's AI management system; ETSI EN 304 223 addresses baseline cybersecurity for AI models and systems. They support different review questions.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specifies requirements for establishing and improving an AI management system. ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1, published in December 2025, sets out lifecycle security requirements; ETSI's January 2026 announcement describes 13 principles across five phases.

For procurement, identify the organisation, system, version, intended use and applicable requirements first. Then ask which records support each requirement and what remains untested. Council's scoped measurement records can contribute evidence where the method is relevant. A signed card or a thematic crosswalk does not establish conformity with either complete standard, certify an organisation, or prove a system secure.

Reviewed 4 November 2026. Use the applicable standard edition and an agreed assessment scope.

title: SCITT: signed statements and receipts
body:
SCITT separates a signed claim from the receipt showing its registration with a transparency service. That distinction helps reviewers inspect provenance without confusing it with truth.

RFC 9943 describes the SCITT architecture. Signed Statements use COSE_Sign1; a Transparency Service can issue a receipt that is combined with a statement. A signed JSON record does not become a SCITT Transparent Statement merely because it has a signature. The RFC also explains that issuers can make false statements.

Council publishes signed measurement evidence in its own formats. For any proposed SCITT integration, inspect the exact conversion, issuer key, identified service, registration policy and verifiable receipt before claiming interoperability. Preserve the original artifact and method references so a reviewer can compare the claim with the measurement. This explainer does not assert that Council's published JSON cards are SCITT-registered.

Reviewed 4 November 2026.

title: FedRAMP: machine-readable evidence
body:
FedRAMP evidence formats and transition dates depend on the applicable programme rules. There is no universal September 30 OSCAL deadline established by this explainer.

The final FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026 list 1 January 2027 as the general mandatory-adoption milestone, subject to specific applicability and effective dates. Rev5 rule FRC-CSO-JSN requires JSON valid against a corresponding FedRAMP schema when a rule supplies one, unless that rule specifies otherwise. Check the selected path, class, applicable rules and current transition provisions before preparing a submission.

Structured evidence can make a review easier to reproduce, but format validation, cryptographic integrity, assessment and the authority's decision are separate checks. Council measurement records may support a defined evidence question; they do not constitute a FedRAMP package, accepted assessment or authorisation by themselves. Agree any mapping and delivery scope with the responsible provider and assessor.

Reviewed 4 November 2026; this replaces the earlier generic September 30 framing.

title: Council of Europe AI Treaty: scope and status
body:
The Council of Europe AI Framework Convention concerns human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the AI lifecycle. It addresses obligations of its Parties.

CETS No. 225 opened for signature on 5 September 2024. Its entry-into-force mechanism requires five ratifications, including at least three Council of Europe member States. The Convention addresses matters including remedies and risk assessment. What a private organisation must do depends on the applicable domestic measures and jurisdiction; the treaty does not require use of Council of AI products.

For current signatures, ratifications, declarations and entry-into-force status, consult the Treaty Office chart. This explainer does not repeat the September 2026 count as a current observation. Council's previous dated correction remains available in its corrections ledger.

A practical evidence review can identify the system, affected people, decision, relevant records and unresolved questions. That work supports scrutiny; it does not determine treaty compliance.

Reviewed 4 November 2026. No new live ratification count is asserted.
references: Council corrections ledger, including C-2026-0929-03 — https://councilof.ai/api/corrections

title: Colorado AI: current rules and evidence
body:
Colorado's automated decision-making and chatbot requirements have changed since the original 2024 legislation. Start with the current enacted laws and Attorney General's rulemaking record.

The Attorney General identifies SB26-189 as replacing the earlier high-risk AI provisions and HB26-1263 as the Chatbot Safety Act. Both have requirements taking effect on 1 January 2027. The latter includes AI disclosure and safeguards for conversational AI users. The rulemaking page records a 26 October 2026 hearing; the draft-rule documents should not be described as final rules merely because that hearing occurred.

Identify the service, users, consequential decisions and applicable operator duties before mapping evidence. A measurement packet can document observed behaviour under a stated method; it does not replace a required disclosure, human-review process or legal applicability assessment. Council does not determine compliance through a signed score.

Reviewed 4 November 2026. This replaces the earlier chatbot reference to C.R.S. 6-1-716, which concerns security-breach notification.

title: NIST AI 600-1: evidence mapping
body:
NIST AI 600-1 is a generative AI companion to the voluntary AI Risk Management Framework. It helps organisations select risk-management actions appropriate to their context.

NIST published the profile on 26 July 2024. To use it in an evidence review, identify the relevant risk and suggested action, assign an owner, and link the supporting records and remaining questions. A test result should name its system version, inputs, method, date and limitations.

Federal deployment has additional, separately applicable requirements. A signed model card does not automatically satisfy both NIST guidance and FedRAMP rules, and this page establishes no complete crosswalk between them. Council's published instruments and records can support a scoped measurement task where relevant; the responsible organisation still needs to determine applicability, assess the evidence and complete the required process.

Reviewed 4 November 2026. NIST AI 600-1 is a published profile, not the earlier draft.
references: NIST AI RMF and Generative AI Profile — https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework

title: EU AI Act Article 5: prohibited practices
body:
Article 5 of the EU AI Act identifies prohibited practices through defined conditions and, for some provisions, specific exceptions. Read the current text for the proposed use.

An evidence review should begin with intended purpose, affected people, deployment context and the behaviour in question. Record which provision may apply, what observations support the analysis and what needs legal or technical investigation. Avoid treating a short list of categories as a complete applicability test.

Council's instruments can produce bounded observations where a test method is relevant. Passing a finite test bank cannot demonstrate that every prohibited pathway is absent from a system. A signed result also does not legalise an otherwise prohibited practice or establish Article 5 compliance. A useful packet keeps the observed result, the provider's claims and the applicability decision separate.

Reviewed 4 November 2026 against the Commission's current Article 5 reference; verify the applicable legal text before a deployment decision.
references: European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 5 — https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-5
Council measurement scope and limitations — https://councilof.ai/honesty/

title: EU AI Act Article 50(2): marking evidence
body:
Article 50(2) addresses providers of AI systems generating synthetic content. It requires machine-readable marking and detectability, subject to its scope and exceptions.

The provision describes effectiveness, interoperability, robustness and reliability as far as technically feasible. It does not itself prescribe Council's signature format, a universal model-identity field, or an independent signature on every output. Other Article 50 duties concern different actors and uses, so identify the relevant paragraph first.

A scoped evidence task can inspect named outputs, preserve their bytes and metadata, record the detector or verifier used, and report results and limitations. Council can describe such observations without equating a detected marker with factual truth or safety. A signed measurement record documents the observation; it does not replace the applicable marking duty or establish complete compliance.

Reviewed 4 November 2026. Use the current Article 50 text and implementation guidance for applicability and timing.
references: European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 50 — https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-50
Council measurement scope and limitations — https://councilof.ai/honesty/

title: EU AI Act Article 6: risk classification
body:
Article 6 classifies high-risk AI by reference to product-related conditions and Annex III uses. Classification depends on the system and intended use, including applicable exceptions.

A useful review records the product or use case, role of the organisation, relevant provision, reasoned assessment and supporting material. Check the current consolidated text, guidance and application dates; a generic score cannot determine the classification. Where a provider relies on the Annex III exception, the relevant assessment and registration requirements must also be examined.

Council measurement records may inform a specific technical question in that review. They do not replace classification reasoning, risk management, documentation or any applicable conformity process. No measurement credential is presented here as the strongest or sufficient evidence for every system. Identify what each record establishes and the decisions that remain with the responsible people.

Reviewed 4 November 2026 against the Commission's current Article 6 reference.
references: European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 6 — https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6
Council measurement scope and limitations — https://councilof.ai/honesty/

title: Monitored containment: scope and evidence
body:
Monitored containment describes a proposed operating posture: define a boundary, observe relevant events and review evidence of failures or changes. Coverage must be demonstrated for the named deployment.

A useful record identifies the system, boundary, observation period, capture method, event and limitations. Missing observations, an unavailable source and a tested failure are different outcomes. A monitoring design or a published index alone does not establish continuous observation, a staffed response service or successful remediation.

Council's measurement and verification tools help readers inspect specific published records. Cryptographic verification can establish record integrity under the applicable trust assumptions; it does not establish that every event was captured, that the recorded claim is true, or that a boundary cannot be crossed. Operational monitoring and incident handling require their own implemented controls, permissions and accountable people.

Reviewed 4 November 2026. Read the scope and date of each linked result before relying on it.
references: Council measurement scope and limitations — https://councilof.ai/honesty/

title: Signed measurement cards: how to verify
body:
A Council measurement card records an issuer's measurement claim. Verifying its signature checks the signed bytes against the expected key; it does not independently repeat the measurement.

Obtain the exact record and identify its format, signing key and verification procedure. Use the browser verifier or the documented script only for the record profiles it supports. Pin the expected public key from the published trust information, rather than trusting a replacement key supplied inside an arbitrary file. Read hash integrity, signature validity, inclusion and current board admission as separate results where the format distinguishes them.

The verifier reports VALID, INVALID or UNCHECKABLE for the check performed. A missing key or unsupported profile must remain unresolved rather than be treated as a successful check. Read the underlying method, evidence, date and corrections to assess the measurement claim. Neither a valid signature nor a signed card certifies a model's safety or legal compliance.

Reviewed 4 November 2026 against the published verification instructions and verifier source.
references: Council verification instructions and profile limits — https://councilof.ai/signed/HOW-TO-VERIFY.md

title: Council Signal: governance measurement
body:
Council Signal describes the measurement work behind Council's published evidence: turn a stated governance question into an inspectable procedure and a bounded result.

Published GSPC instruments use specified banks and scoring methods. Read the exact method and version for the result in question; do not assume every declared axis has been measured or that different instruments are interchangeable. Current board admission and measurement states come from /api/gspc. Ties and unmeasured cells remain explicit.

Selected records are signed so another reader can verify their integrity. That verification is separate from reproducing the experiment, evaluating the method or deciding whether the result is relevant to a deployment. A signed record does not imply an independent Council vote, legal authority or a safety certification. Users can inspect the methods, test a supported record and consult corrections without purchasing a favourable result.

Reviewed 4 November 2026.
